name: Kagyu (the Kagyu transmissions: Marpa / Dakpo Kagyu, with the Shangpa grouped by name)
alt_names: bka' brgyud (Tibetan): 'lineage of the (Buddha's) word' / 'of the transmitted precepts'
dkar brgyud, 'the white lineage' (after the white cotton cloth of the repa yogins; an etymology the tradition also gives)
Dakpo Kagyu (dwags po bka' brgyud, after Gampopa of Dakpo)
the four great and eight lesser Kagyu (bka' brgyud che bzhi chung brgyad)
regions: Gungthang, Lapchi, Chubar and Mount Kailash (Milarepa's retreats)

tradition.text: from the buddha Vajradhara to Tilopa (988–1069 by the usual Tibetan reckoning) and Nāropa; Marpa's three (or four) journeys to India in the 11th c.; Milarepa (1040–1123 in Tsangnyön Heruka's reckoning); Gampopa (1079–1153) unites the streams at Daklha Gampo (1121)

scholarly.text: 11th c. (Marpa's translations) onward; the Dakpo Kagyu schools founded in the 12th–13th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Mahāmudrā songs and instructions of Saraha, Śavaripa, Tilopa and Maitrīpa (the dohā cycles; the amanasikāra cycle) and the six dharmas of Tilopa and Nāropa
transmissions_received.evidence: Tōh 2303, 2330, 2331, 2332, 2338 translated by Nāropa/Marpa (colophons read locally); the Kagyu lineage prayers name Tilopa, Nāropa and Maitrīpa

transmissions_received.what: the Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara, Guhyasamāja, Mahāmāyā and Catuḥpīṭha tantras with their empowerments, received by Marpa from Nāropa, Maitrīpa, Kukkuripa and others
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account (Life of Marpa); the translator colophons of Marpa in the Tengyur

transmissions_received.what: the graded path, mind training and monastic discipline, merged by Gampopa with Mahāmudrā ('the two streams of Kadam and Mahāmudrā mixed')
transmissions_received.evidence: Gampopa's Jewel Ornament follows the Kadam graded-path pattern; tradition's account of his Kadam training before meeting Milarepa

transmissions_received.what: the Ratnagotravibhāga as the treatise of sūtra Mahāmudrā
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's report (Gö Lotsāwa, Blue Annals; Jamgön Kongtrul) that Gampopa named the Uttaratantra the treatise of his Mahāmudrā

transmissions_received.what: Dzogchen instructions (Rangjung Dorje's Karma Nyingthig; the Mahāmudrā–Dzogchen union of Karma Chagmé and Tselé Natsok Rangdröl)
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account; see brw:dzogchen-and-mahamudra

transmissions_given.what: the Six Yogas of Nāropa (Tsongkhapa's commentary) and a Mahāmudrā lineage (the 'Ganden oral lineage' Mahāmudrā of the First Panchen Lama)
the Kagyu and Shangpa transmissions collected and revived by Jamgön Kongtrul
mixed Kagyu–Nyingma traditions (Surmang, Nedo; the Mahāmudrā–Dzogchen union)

distinctive_positions: Mahāmudrā — the nature of one's own mind, empty and luminous, the co-emergent dharmakāya — is to be recognized directly through the guru's pointing-out instruction and blessing, then stabilized through the four yogas (one-pointedness, simplicity, one taste, non-meditation).

Two paths: the path of method (the Six Yogas of Nāropa, on the basis of tantric empowerment) and the path of liberation (Mahāmudrā); in Gampopa's system Mahāmudrā may also be introduced on a sūtra basis ('sūtra Mahāmudrā'), a claim contested by Sakya Paṇḍita (dsp:sutra-mahamudra).

Devotion to the guru is 'the head of meditation'; the blessing passes through an unbroken 'golden rosary' of masters each said to have realized the teaching before transmitting it (the 'practice lineage').
Thoughts are not to be suppressed: their nature is dharmakāya (Dorje Chang Thungma); appearances are 'the light of the dharmakāya' (the co-emergent instruction).
Gampopa united the Kadam graded path (the four thoughts, refuge, bodhicitta, the perfections) with Mahāmudrā: renunciation and compassion are the ground on which the view is pointed out.
Renunciation of worldly concerns and long solitary practice in mountain retreats (Milarepa's model) make buddhahood possible in one life and one body.
The recognized reincarnation (tulku) of teachers begins with the Karmapas (tradition's account).
summary: The Kagyu ('lineage of the word') are the Tibetan Buddhist transmissions that descend from the Indian siddhas Tilopa, Nāropa and Maitrīpa through the translator Marpa, the yogin Milarepa and the monk-physician Gampopa, whose disciples founded the 'four great and eight lesser' Dakpo Kagyu schools (Karma, Tsalpa, Barom, Phagdru; Drikung, Drukpa, Taklung, Trophu, Martsang, Yelpa, Yazang, Shugseb). Their hallmark is Mahāmudrā — direct recognition of the mind's nature through the guru's blessing — together with the Six Yogas of Nāropa. The separate Shangpa Kagyu, from the ḍākinīs Niguma and Sukhasiddhi through Khyungpo Naljor, is grouped with them by name.
notes: Umbrella id: each school below counts as its own root for convergence. The Shangpa is not descended from Marpa; it is placed under the Kagyu grouping only because the tradition calls it 'Kagyu' and the registry assigns it here.

name: Karma Kagyu (Kamtsang Kagyu)
regions: Kampo Nenang, Karma Gön and Tsurphu (founded by Düsum Khyenpa)

tradition.text: founded by the first Karmapa Düsum Khyenpa (1110–1193), who founded Kampo Nenang (1164), Karma Gön (1185) and Tsurphu (c. 1187–1189)

transmissions_received.what: Gampopa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas, through Düsum Khyenpa
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's lineage lists (the Karma Kagyu 'golden rosary')

transmissions_received.what: the Vima Nyingthig / Karma Nyingthig through Rangjung Dorje (from Rigdzin Kumārarāja); the Nedo branch's Kagyu–Nyingma synthesis
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account

transmissions_received.what: the other-emptiness (shentong) reading of buddha-nature in one strand (the 8th Situ, Jamgön Kongtrul), contested by others in the school
transmissions_received.evidence: see dsp:rangtong-shentong

transmissions_given.what: Jamgön Kongtrul's collections (the Kagyu Ngagdzö; the Treasury of Instructions) and the three-year retreat model

distinctive_positions: The Karmapa, recognized in successive rebirths since Karma Pakshi (the first recognized tulku line by the tradition's account), heads the school; the black crown is his emblem.

Mahāmudrā is taught in the system of the 9th Karmapa's three manuals (Ocean of Definitive Meaning, Dispelling the Darkness of Ignorance, Pointing Out the Dharmakāya): preliminaries, śamatha, vipaśyanā, pointing-out, and the four yogas.
Rangjung Dorje's teaching on the nature of mind: buddha-nature is mind's luminous clarity-emptiness; the eight consciousnesses are distinguished from the five wisdoms into which they are transformed.
Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen are of one essence (Rangjung Dorje; Karma Chagmé's union of the two).

Within the school the Madhyamaka of the 8th Karmapa (the Chariot of the Dakpo Kagyu Siddhas) and the shentong reading of the 3rd Karmapa's buddha-nature teaching as understood by the 8th Situ and Jamgön Kongtrul coexist (not yet reconciled; see dsp:rangtong-shentong).
summary: The school founded by the first Karmapa, Düsum Khyenpa, a principal disciple of Gampopa, and headed by the successive Karmapas; the largest Kagyu school, centred on Tsurphu and on the great monasteries of Kham, and in exile on Rumtek. Its Mahāmudrā system is that of the 3rd, 8th and 9th Karmapas; its later renaissance came through the 8th Situ and Jamgön Kongtrul.
notes: The recognition of the 17th Karmapa is contested between two candidates (Ogyen Trinley Dorje and Trinley Thaye Dorje); recorded as metadata only (recent).

name: Drikung Kagyu
regions: the retreat mountains Kailash, Lapchi and Tsari

tradition.text: founded by Jigten Sumgön (1143–1217), disciple of Phagmodrupa, at Drikung Thil in 1179

transmissions_received.what: Phagmodrupa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account: Jigten Sumgön was Phagmodrupa's disciple

distinctive_positions: The 'single intent' (dgongs gcig): all the Buddha's teachings share one intent; the three vows (prātimokṣa, bodhisattva, mantra) are one in essence (dsp:three-vows-one-essence).
The fivefold Mahāmudrā (phyag chen lnga ldan): bodhicitta, the deity body, devotion to the guru, the Mahāmudrā view, and dedication — the five together make the practice complete.
The Drikung transference (phowa) is famous; great public phowa gatherings are held (recent practice, earlier roots).
summary: One of the 'eight lesser' Kagyu schools founded by disciples of Phagmodrupa; established by Jigten Sumgön at Drikung Thil, known for the Gongchig ('Single Intent') and the fivefold Mahāmudrā, for sending retreatants to Kailash, Lapchi and Tsari, and for its phowa.
notes: Parent set to the Kagyu umbrella (not Phagdru) so that the school counts as its own root; its descent from Phagmodrupa is recorded under transmissions_received.

name: Drukpa Kagyu
alt_names: Upper, Middle and Lower Drukpa (stod 'brug, bar 'brug, smad 'brug)
regions: Bhutan (state tradition since the Zhabdrung, 17th c.)

tradition.text: founded by Tsangpa Gyare Yeshe Dorje (1161–1211), who at Namdruk saw thunder-dragons (druk) and so named the school

transmissions_received.what: Mahāmudrā through Lingje Repa, disciple of Phagmodrupa
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account

transmissions_received.what: the Rechung hearing-lineage teachings, 'rediscovered' by Tsangpa Gyare as the Six Equal Tastes
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account

distinctive_positions: The 'six cycles of equal taste' (ro snyoms skor drug) and the 'seven auspicious coincidences' (rten 'brel rab bdun), rediscovered by Tsangpa Gyare: adversity, illness and death are carried onto the path.

The renunciate mountain-retreat ideal of Milarepa (the Upper Drukpa of Götsangpa); the tradition's saying that half the people are Drukpa, half the Drukpa are beggars, and half the beggars are siddhas.
Pema Karpo's systematization of Mahāmudrā and the Six Yogas; the 'divine madmen' (Tsangnyön Heruka, Drukpa Kunley) whose unconventional conduct is read as teaching.
summary: One of the 'eight lesser' Kagyu schools, founded by Tsangpa Gyare at Ralung and Druk; divided into Upper, Middle and Lower branches; its Southern branch became the state tradition of Bhutan under Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal. Known for renunciate retreat practice, Pema Karpo's writings and the divine madmen.

name: Shangpa Kagyu
alt_names: the Shangpa (after the Shang valley in Tsang)
regions: later carried inside the Jonang (Tāranātha), Karma Kagyu and Rimé (Jamgön Kongtrul); revived in the 20th c. by Kalu Rinpoche

tradition.text: Khyungpo Naljor (by the tradition's reckoning 978/990–1127/1139, a life of over a century) received the teachings in India from the ḍākinīs Niguma and Sukhasiddhi

transmissions_received.what: Niguma's six dharmas, the Amulet Mahāmudrā and related cycles; Sukhasiddhi's teachings
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account

transmissions_received.what: Khyungpo Naljor's earlier Bön and Dzogchen training
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account (biographies)

transmissions_given.what: the Shangpa cycles held and commented on by Tāranātha
the Shangpa texts collected by Jamgön Kongtrul

distinctive_positions: Its source is two women: the ḍākinīs Niguma (by the Tibetan account Nāropa's sister or consort) and Sukhasiddhi, received by Khyungpo Naljor in India.

The 'five golden dharmas' pictured as a tree: the root, Niguma's six dharmas; the trunk, the Amulet Mahāmudrā; the branches, the three integrations; the flowers, the white and red Khecarī; the fruit, the deathless body and mind.
By Niguma's command (tradition) the teachings passed to a single disciple for the first seven generations (the 'seven jewels'), then spread widely.
The Shangpa has had no large institutional school of its own after the 14th c.; it lives inside other schools.
summary: A Tibetan transmission distinct from the Marpa Kagyu, founded by Khyungpo Naljor on the teachings of the Indian ḍākinīs Niguma and Sukhasiddhi; its 'five golden dharmas' parallel the Six Yogas and Mahāmudrā. It survives within the Karma Kagyu, Jonang and Rimé and was revived by Kalu Rinpoche.
notes: Grouped under lin:kagyu by name only (see the umbrella's note).

name: Tsalpa Kagyu

tradition.text: founded by Zhang Yudrakpa Tsöndrü Drakpa (Lama Zhang, 1123–1193), disciple of Gampopa's nephew Gomtsul

scholarly.text: late 12th c.; the Tshalpa myriarchy flourished in the 13th–14th c.

distinctive_positions: Lama Zhang's Mahāmudrā instruction, including the 'white self-sufficient remedy' (dkar po chig thub) idiom that Sakya Paṇḍita attacked.
summary: One of the 'four great' Dakpo Kagyu schools, founded by Lama Zhang, author of the Ultimate Supreme Path of Mahāmudrā; the school later merged into others.

transmissions_received.what: Gampopa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account of the 'four great' schools

name: Barom Kagyu

tradition.text: founded by Barom Darma Wangchuk, disciple of Gampopa

distinctive_positions: Gampopa's Mahāmudrā as transmitted by Barom Darma Wangchuk.
summary: One of the 'four great' Dakpo Kagyu schools, founded by Barom Darma Wangchuk; survives in Nangchen.

transmissions_received.what: Gampopa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account of the 'four great' schools

name: Phagdru Kagyu

tradition.text: founded by Phagmodrupa Dorje Gyalpo (1110–1170), disciple of Gampopa (and earlier of Sachen Kunga Nyingpo)

scholarly.text: mid-12th c.; the Phagmodru ruling house from 1354

distinctive_positions: Phagmodrupa joined Gampopa's Mahāmudrā with the Sakya Lamdre he had studied under Sachen.
summary: One of the 'four great' Dakpo Kagyu schools, founded by Phagmodrupa at Densa Thil; the eight 'lesser' schools (Drikung, Drukpa, Taklung, Trophu, Martsang, Yelpa, Yazang, Shugseb) were founded by his disciples.

transmissions_received.what: Gampopa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account of the 'four great' schools

transmissions_received.what: the Lamdre, studied by Phagmodrupa under Sachen Kunga Nyingpo
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account

notes: sub_lineages lists the eight schools descended from Phagmodrupa's disciples; their parent field points to the Kagyu umbrella so that each counts as its own root.

name: Taklung Kagyu

tradition.text: founded by Taklung Thangpa Tashi Pal (1142–1210), disciple of Phagmodrupa

distinctive_positions: Emphasis on strict discipline within the Phagdru Mahāmudrā tradition.
summary: One of the 'eight lesser' Kagyu schools, founded by Taklung Thangpa at Taklung; known for strict monastic discipline.

transmissions_received.what: Phagmodrupa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account of the 'eight lesser' schools

name: Trophu Kagyu

tradition.text: founded by Gyaltsa Rinchen Gön and Kunden Repa, disciples of Phagmodrupa; later Trophu Lotsāwa invited Śākyaśrībhadra to Tibet

distinctive_positions: Transmits the Dakpo Kagyu Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas received from Phagmodrupa; no distinctive doctrine recorded here.
summary: One of the 'eight lesser' Kagyu schools, centred on Trophu in Tsang; now extinct as a separate school.

transmissions_received.what: Phagmodrupa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account of the 'eight lesser' schools

name: Martsang Kagyu

tradition.text: founded by Marpa Drubthob Sherab Senge, disciple of Phagmodrupa

distinctive_positions: Transmits the Dakpo Kagyu Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas received from Phagmodrupa; no distinctive doctrine recorded here.
summary: One of the 'eight lesser' Kagyu schools; extinct.

transmissions_received.what: Phagmodrupa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account of the 'eight lesser' schools

name: Yelpa Kagyu

tradition.text: founded by Drubthob Yelpa Yeshe Tsek, disciple of Phagmodrupa

distinctive_positions: Transmits the Dakpo Kagyu Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas received from Phagmodrupa; no distinctive doctrine recorded here.
summary: One of the 'eight lesser' Kagyu schools; absorbed.

transmissions_received.what: Phagmodrupa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account of the 'eight lesser' schools

name: Yazang Kagyu

tradition.text: founded by Zarawa Kalden Yeshe Senge, disciple of Phagmodrupa

distinctive_positions: Transmits the Dakpo Kagyu Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas received from Phagmodrupa; no distinctive doctrine recorded here.
summary: One of the 'eight lesser' Kagyu schools; extinct.

transmissions_received.what: Phagmodrupa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account of the 'eight lesser' schools

name: Shugseb Kagyu

tradition.text: founded by Gyergom Tsultrim Senge, disciple of Phagmodrupa

distinctive_positions: Transmits the Dakpo Kagyu Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas received from Phagmodrupa; no distinctive doctrine recorded here.
summary: One of the 'eight lesser' Kagyu schools; its seat Shugseb later became a Nyingma nunnery.

transmissions_received.evidence: tradition's account of the 'eight lesser' schools
